120.title: Ramadan: the new moon
120.hook: the month begins when the crescent is seen or the month is counted
120.howItsDone: Muslims begin and end Ramadan by the new crescent moon: some communities wait for a local sighting, some follow a sighting elsewhere, and some use astronomical calculation, so start dates can differ by a day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: salawat, blessings on the Prophet, one sent and ten returned. Your line was peace on him.

The evening after the twenty-ninth day of the month before Ramadan. Just after sunset, on a hill outside a city, a small group stands facing west with binoculars, squinting where the sun just went down. In a family group chat, someone keeps asking: is it tomorrow? Has anyone seen it? Somewhere else, a committee is on the phone with people in three countries. Everyone's looking for the same thing: a thread of light, thinner than a fingernail clipping, low in the sky for a few minutes before it sets.
screen: `FACING WEST AFTER SUNSET.` → `IS IT TOMORROW?` → `A THREAD OF LIGHT.`

segments.voice: That thread is the hilal, the crescent: the first sliver of the new moon. The Islamic calendar is lunar. Each month begins with the hilal and lasts twenty-nine or thirty days, which is why Ramadan moves about eleven days earlier every year, as you heard on day six. The Qur'an, in Surah al-Baqarah, says people ask about the new moons, and answers that they are markers of time for people, and for the pilgrimage. The sky is the calendar. A hadith in Bukhari gives the rule: fast when you see it, and stop fasting when you see it; and if clouds hide it from you, complete the month as thirty days. Simple on a clear night in Medina. Harder for Muslims spread across every time zone. So Muslims today follow different approaches, and they're open about it. Some communities wait for a local sighting, with their own eyes, where they live. Some follow a sighting anywhere in the world, or in a particular country. Some use astronomical calculation to fix the dates ahead of time. That's why two mosques in the same city sometimes start Ramadan a day apart, and why the group chat is so busy. There's also a short prayer from the Prophet ﷺ for the moment the crescent is seen, reported in Tirmidhi: asking that the month come with blessing and faith, with safety and with islam, submission to God, and ending, speaking to the moon itself: my Lord and your Lord is Allah.
screen: `HILAL — THE FIRST SLIVER.` · `MARKERS OF TIME FOR PEOPLE.` · `FAST WHEN YOU SEE IT.` · `SIGHTING, OR COUNTING.` · then, large: `MY LORD AND YOUR LORD IS ALLAH.`

segments.voice: If you can, step outside or to a window after dark and find the moon: a sliver, a half, a full circle, or not there at all. Wherever it is in its month, it's counting days for someone. If it's too early, close your eyes and picture that thin crescent low in the west just after sunset. If you pray, you can say the Prophet's words to it: my Lord and your Lord is Allah.
Hilal. The crescent of the new moon, the first sliver that begins every Islamic month, and Ramadan. Today's word.
Your line: watch for the crescent. Whenever Ramadan comes for you, this is how it starts. One hundred twenty days in.

121.title: Ramadan: the early meal
121.hook: eat before dawn, for there is blessing in it (Bukhari)
121.howItsDone: During Ramadan, Muslims who fast wake before dawn to eat suhur, often dates, water and simple food, and stop eating and drinking at the start of dawn, when the time of fajr begins.

segments.voice: Yesterday: hilal, the crescent of the new moon. Your line was watch for the crescent.

Three forty-five in the morning. In old neighborhoods of Cairo or Istanbul, during Ramadan, a man may still walk the dark streets beating a small drum and calling out names, waking people up. In a suburban kitchen, a phone alarm goes off, and someone stumbles in, eyes half shut, and starts the kettle. Oats. Dates. Eggs. A lot of water. Nobody's hungry at this hour. Everyone's eating anyway. The Prophet ﷺ gave the reason in one line.
screen: `THREE FORTY-FIVE IN THE MORNING.` → `A DRUM IN THE DARK STREETS.` → `NOBODY'S HUNGRY. EVERYONE EATS.`

segments.voice: The meal is called suhur, from sahar, the last part of the night, just before dawn. The line is in Bukhari: take the suhur meal, for in suhur there is blessing. Barakah. More than a benefit: a quiet abundance, when a little turns out to be enough. The practical side is obvious, too: a long day without food or water goes better if you start it fed. But when do you stop? The Qur'an, in Surah al-Baqarah, says eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread of the dawn. And there's a lovely story about that verse, also in Bukhari. A companion named Adi ibn Hatim took it literally. He put a white thread and a black thread under his pillow and kept looking at them all night, waiting to tell them apart. He couldn't. In the morning he told the Prophet, who, in one telling, teased him that his pillow must be very wide, and explained: it means the darkness of the night and the whiteness of the day. The white thread is the first line of light along the horizon. Another companion, Zayd ibn Thabit, said they ate suhur with the Prophet and then stood for the prayer; asked how long between them, he said: about as long as reciting fifty verses. So the meal was late, close to dawn. Not a midnight snack. A small, deliberate meal in the dark, the last thing before the day's long quiet.
screen: `SUHUR — FROM SAHAR, BEFORE DAWN.` · `IN SUHUR THERE IS BLESSING.` · `A WHITE THREAD AND A BLACK THREAD.` · `ABOUT FIFTY VERSES BEFORE THE PRAYER.` · then, large: `A SMALL MEAL, IN THE DARK, ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: Picture tomorrow morning, a little earlier than you usually wake: where the glass is, where you'll sit, drinking slowly in the dark before the day starts asking things of you. If you fast, plan your suhur the same way, simple, late, on purpose; if you don't, settle on one glass of water before anything else, and say to yourself: blessing before dawn.
Suhur. The meal before dawn in Ramadan, eaten late, for in it there is blessing. Today's word.

122.title: Ramadan: breaking with a date
122.hook: at sunset, a date and water, and a du'a
122.howItsDone: At sunset during Ramadan, Muslims break the fast promptly, often with dates and water, pray maghrib, and then eat the evening meal, frequently at communal iftars in mosques and homes.

segments.voice: Yesterday: suhur, the meal before dawn, and the two threads. Your line was blessing before dawn.

A long table in a mosque hall, paper cloths, plastic cups. A hundred people sitting down, some who know each other, some who don't: a student far from home, a taxi driver on his break, an elderly couple, a neighbor who isn't Muslim but was invited. Nobody's eating. Every plate has a few dates on it, and a cup of water. Everyone's watching the clock, or listening. Then, from the front, the call to the sunset prayer begins, and a hundred hands reach, at the same moment, for one small date.
screen: `A LONG TABLE, A HUNDRED PEOPLE.` → `A FEW DATES ON EVERY PLATE.` → `A HUNDRED HANDS, ONE MOMENT.`

segments.voice: It's called iftar, from a root meaning to break open, to split: the meal that breaks the fast at sunset, as maghrib comes in. The way it starts goes back to the Prophet ﷺ. A companion, Anas, said the Prophet would break his fast with fresh dates before praying; if there were none, with dried dates; if none, with a few sips of water. That's all. Not a feast first. Something small and sweet, and water. The feast, if there is one, comes after. And there's a good kind of hurry to it. A hadith in Bukhari says people will remain in good as long as they hasten to break the fast. The point isn't to linger and prove strength. When the sun's gone, the fast is done. There's a short prayer reported for the moment, in the Sunan of Abu Dawud: the thirst has gone, the veins are moistened, and the reward is confirmed, if Allah wills. Three plain facts, said with a date still in your mouth. Then the line that makes it sweet. In Bukhari, the Prophet said the fasting person has two joys: one when they break their fast, and one when they meet their Lord. The first is right there at the table. And the tradition prizes sharing it. A hadith in Tirmidhi says whoever gives food to a fasting person to break their fast has the same reward as the one who fasted, without taking anything away from theirs. That's why mosques set out those long tables, and why strangers get invited.
screen: `IFTAR — TO BREAK OPEN.` · `FRESH DATES, DRIED DATES, OR WATER.` · `HASTEN TO BREAK THE FAST.` · `TWO JOYS.` · then, large: `FEED ONE, SHARE THE REWARD.`

segments.voice: Before your next meal, even if your fast is only the hours since you last ate, sit down and take something small and sweet first, a date if you have one or a piece of fruit, and a glass of water. Eat it slowly, noticing the first taste of sweetness and the water going down, and wait a moment before the rest. If you pray, you can say bismillah first.
Iftar. The meal that breaks the fast at sunset: a date, water, a few words, and the first of two joys. Today's word.

123.title: Ramadan: the night prayers
123.hook: long night prayers in the mosque, the whole Qur'an recited over the month
123.howItsDone: During Ramadan, many Sunni Muslims gather after the night prayer for tarawih, eight or twenty rak'ahs led by a reciter who often completes the whole Qur'an over the month; many Shia Muslims pray extra Ramadan night prayers individually.

segments.voice: Yesterday: iftar, breaking the fast with a date and water, the first of two joys. Your line was sweet at sunset.

Ten at night in Ramadan, and the mosque parking lot is fuller than on a Friday. Inside, rows of people, shoulder to shoulder, standing. At the front, one voice is reciting, page after page, clear and long. Kids fall asleep on the carpet at the back. A grandmother sits on a chair by the wall. The standing lasts an hour, sometimes more. In mosques that recite a portion each night, someone who came every night would have heard the whole Qur'an by the month's end, cover to cover.
screen: `TEN AT NIGHT, A FULL PARKING LOT.` → `ONE VOICE, PAGE AFTER PAGE.` → `COVER TO COVER BY MONTH'S END.`

segments.voice: These prayers are called tarawih. The name, tradition says, comes from a word for rest, because those who prayed them long ago would sit and rest after every four units. The prayer is voluntary, not one of the five, but in Ramadan it has a special place. A hadith in Bukhari says: whoever stands in prayer in Ramadan out of faith and hoping for reward, their past sins are forgiven. Here's how it began. Aisha said that one Ramadan the Prophet ﷺ prayed at night in the mosque, and some people prayed behind him. The next night more came, and the next, more still. Then one night the mosque was full, and he didn't come out. In the morning he explained: I saw what you were doing, and nothing kept me away except that I feared it would be made obligatory on you. He didn't want to turn a gift into a burden. Years later, the second caliph, Umar, walked into the mosque one Ramadan night and found people praying in scattered little groups, each behind a different reciter. He gathered them behind one, a companion named Ubayy ibn Ka'b. The next night, seeing them all together, he said: what a fine new thing this is. How many units? Communities differ, openly. Some pray eight, following a report from Aisha. Others pray twenty, as in the great mosque in Mecca. In Shia practice, the extra night prayers of Ramadan are prayed alone, not in congregation. The numbers differ; the shape doesn't. The days of Ramadan are for fasting. The nights are for standing.
screen: `TARAWIH — FROM A WORD FOR REST.` · `STAND IN RAMADAN, OUT OF FAITH.` · `HE FEARED IT WOULD BE MADE A DUTY.` · `UMAR GATHERED THEM BEHIND ONE.` · then, large: `EIGHT, OR TWENTY, OR ALONE.`

segments.voice: Before bed, stand still for a minute or two, feet planted, hands folded or at your sides. If you pray, add two voluntary rak'ahs, or make one standing a little longer than usual, reciting slowly; if you don't, stand in a quiet room and listen to the house at night, how different it feels from the day. When your legs ask to sit, stay one breath longer.
Tarawih. The long night prayers of Ramadan, named for the rests between them, the Qur'an recited over the month. Today's word.
Your line: the nights are for standing. Page after page, the Qur'an keeps going. Day one hundred twenty-three, done.

124.title: Ramadan: the Night of Power
124.hook: a night better than a thousand months, sought in the last ten (97:1–5)
124.tomorrow: Ramadan: the fast of the tongue
124.howItsDone: In the last ten nights of Ramadan, Muslims seek Laylat al-Qadr with extra prayer, Qur'an recitation and supplication, especially on the odd nights and often the twenty-seventh, and some stay in the mosque in retreat (i'tikaf).

segments.voice: Yesterday: tarawih, the long night prayers, named for their rests. Your line was the nights are for standing.

A thousand months is about eighty-three years. A whole lifetime, most of one anyway. Somewhere in the next ten nights there's one night worth more than all of that. Nobody says which. Only that it's one of them, probably an odd one. What would anyone do? In the last ten nights of Ramadan, the answer is easy to see: stay up, show up, try not to miss it. Mosques stay full past midnight. Some people don't go home at all.
screen: `A THOUSAND MONTHS: A LIFETIME.` → `ONE NIGHT WORTH MORE.` → `YOU'RE NOT TOLD WHICH.`

segments.voice: It's called Laylat al-Qadr. Laylah is night. Qadr is harder to translate: power, measure, decree, worth. Pickthall calls it the Night of Power. It has its own short surah, al-Qadr, five verses. It says this was the night the Qur'an was sent down, then asks: what will make you understand what the Night of Power is? And answers: "The Night of Power is better than a thousand months." The angels and the Spirit come down in it, by their Lord's permission, and it is peace until the rising of the dawn. So Muslims remember it as the night the revelation began, the night in the cave of Hira you met back in camp two. But which night? A hadith in Bukhari says seek it in the odd nights of the last ten: the twenty-first, twenty-third, twenty-fifth, twenty-seventh, twenty-ninth. Some give special weight to the twenty-seventh, others to other nights. And there's a story about why nobody knows for sure. In Bukhari, the Prophet ﷺ came out one night to tell the people which night it was. On the way, he found two men quarreling, and the knowledge was taken up from him. He told them: perhaps that is better for you. So the not-knowing became part of the gift: people seek it on all ten. And Aisha once asked him: if I find it, what should I say? He taught her a short line, in Tirmidhi, that asks God, who loves to pardon, to pardon her. Not wealth. Not success. Pardon. On the night worth a lifetime, that was the request.
screen: `LAYLAT AL-QADR — POWER, MEASURE, DECREE.` · `BETTER THAN A THOUSAND MONTHS.` · `SEEK IT IN THE ODD NIGHTS.` · `TAKEN UP, BECAUSE OF A QUARREL.` · then, large: `ON THAT NIGHT, ASK FOR PARDON.`

segments.voice: Before you sleep, sit up in bed or on the floor, lights low, for one minute of quiet you wouldn't have had. If you pray, pray a little more, or ask for pardon the way Aisha was taught; if you don't, simply sit, and let it be a night you didn't let slip past. You don't know which night matters most, so the minute belongs to every one of them.
Laylat al-Qadr. The Night of Power, when the Qur'an was first sent down, better than a thousand months, sought in the last ten nights. Today's word.
Your line: better than a thousand months. Ten nights, and one of them is it. See you tomorrow.

125.title: Ramadan: the fast of the tongue
125.hook: whoever doesn't leave false speech, Allah has no need of his hunger (Bukhari)
125.tomorrow: The charity of the fast's end
125.howItsDone: During Ramadan, Muslims try to fast from lying, gossip, arguing and harsh words as well as from food and drink, and some answer provocation with the words 'I am fasting'.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power. Your line was better than a thousand months.

Four in the afternoon on a Ramadan day. A woman driving home hasn't eaten or drunk since before dawn. Someone cuts her off, hard, then honks, as if it were her fault. Her hands tighten on the wheel. The words are already in her mouth. She's tired, she's hungry, and the other driver is wrong. Her finger is on the window switch. The tradition has a sentence ready for this exact moment. Two words, in Arabic.
screen: `FOUR IN THE AFTERNOON, NO WATER.` → `SOMEONE CUTS HER OFF.` → `THE WORDS ARE RIGHT THERE.`

segments.voice: Back on day six, you heard a hadith from Bukhari about Ramadan. Here it is again, because today it's the whole point: whoever does not give up false speech and acting on it, Allah has no need of their giving up food and drink. The stomach isn't the only thing that fasts. A report in the Sunan of Ibn Majah is even blunter: many a person who fasts gets nothing from their fast except hunger. The whole day, and nothing to show but an empty stomach. So what do you do at four in the afternoon, when the words are right there? Another hadith in Bukhari answers: fasting is a shield. If someone fights with you or insults you while you're fasting, say: I am fasting. In Arabic, inni sa'im: two words, said twice. Not to them, necessarily. Maybe to yourself. It's a reminder that what you're doing today is bigger than winning this moment. The word Ramadan, you'll remember, comes from a root for scorching heat. Some scholars have read that as the heat that burns away wrongdoing. Whether or not that's the origin, some Muslims hear the month that way: meant to burn off more than appetite. Gossip. Lying. Complaining. The cutting remark. And the hope is that a month of holding the tongue leaves a habit behind, the way a month of early mornings does.
screen: `NO NEED OF THEIR HUNGER.` · `NOTHING BUT HUNGER.` · `SAY: I AM FASTING. TWICE.` · `A HEAT THAT BURNS AWAY WRONG.` · then, large: `THE TONGUE FASTS TOO.`

segments.voice: Think of the person you're most likely to snap at, or the conversation where your tongue tends to run: the tone, the moment, the words that usually come. Then picture yourself pausing and saying, inside, I am fasting. Whether or not you're fasting from food, you can fast from that one unkind word.
Ramadan. The month of fasting, from a root for scorching heat; a fast of the tongue as well as the stomach. Today's word.
Your line: fast with the tongue too. The shield is two words long. Day one hundred twenty-five, done.

126.title: The charity of the fast's end
126.hook: a small gift of food paid before the Eid prayer so the poor celebrate too
126.howItsDone: Before the Eid al-Fitr prayer, Muslim households give zakat al-fitr for every member, a measure of staple food or, in many communities, its cash value, usually through a mosque that passes it to people in need.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the fast of the tongue, and the two words, I am fasting. Your line was fast with the tongue too.

Tomorrow is the feast. Somewhere tonight, a family is ironing new clothes and making sweets. And somewhere not far away, a family is wondering what there'll be to eat tomorrow at all. It's been a month in a week on this path: a thread of moon low in the west, a meal in the dark before dawn, a date at sunset, long nights of standing, a night worth a lifetime, a fast of the tongue. Now it's almost over. Before the feast can start, the tradition asks for one thing.
screen: `NEW CLOTHES, SWEETS.` → `AND A FAMILY WITH NOTHING.` → `A MONTH IN A WEEK.`

segments.voice: It's called zakat al-fitr, the charity of breaking the fast. A companion, Ibn Umar, describes it in Bukhari. The Prophet ﷺ made it obligatory: a sa' of dates or a sa' of barley, on every Muslim, free or enslaved, man or woman, young or old, paid before people go out to the Eid prayer. A sa' was a measure of volume, about four double handfuls: two cupped hands, filled, four times. Enough food for a family's day. Notice who it's on. Everyone, not only the wealthy, like the yearly zakat you met in camp one. The head of a household pays for each person in it, even a baby born that month. Almost everyone gives; the poorest receive. Why? Another companion, Ibn Abbas, gives two reasons in the Sunan of Abu Dawud. It purifies the one who fasted from any idle or hurtful talk that slipped through the month; a kind of closing apology for yesterday's lesson. And it's food for the poor. Then the timing: paid before the prayer, it's zakat al-fitr. Paid after, it's just ordinary charity. The deadline is the point: the gift has to arrive in time for the poor to celebrate too, not the day after. Today most Muslims give its value, often through a mosque, which buys food or passes on the money. Schools differ on whether money counts or it must be food; the Hanafi school has long allowed money. But the aim hasn't changed in fourteen centuries. Nobody should be hungry on the feast.
screen: `A SA' OF DATES OR BARLEY.` · `ON EVERY MUSLIM, EVEN A BABY.` · `IT PURIFIES, AND IT FEEDS.` · `BEFORE THE PRAYER, NOT AFTER.` · then, large: `NOBODY HUNGRY ON THE FEAST.`

segments.voice: Cup your two hands in front of you, as if holding grain, and fill them in your mind four times: that's a sa', food on someone's table tomorrow. Think of one real way a meal's worth could reach someone: a food bank, a neighbor, a coworker who's struggling, a mosque's collection. If you pray, you can ask that it reach someone in time.
Zakat al-fitr. The charity at the end of the fast: food given by nearly everyone, before the Eid prayer, so the poor celebrate too. Today's word.
Your line: everyone eats on eid. The gift has to arrive in time. A week, done.
